title: Master Shandao's Three Teachings
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Master Shandao is the incarnation of Amitābha, and his words are the words of Amitābha Buddha. For the study and practice of the Pure Land school, he gave three extremely important instructions: 1. single-minded recitation of the name; 2. continuity brings rebirth; 3. even down to ten recitations.

inline.s: Master Shandao is the incarnation of Amitābha,
and his words are the words of Amitābha Buddha

. For the study and practice of the Pure Land school, he gave three extremely important instructions: 1. single-minded recitation of the name; 2. continuity brings rebirth; 3. even down to ten recitations.

This is the essence of Pure Land practice. A reciter of the Buddha who holds fast to it without forgetting and diligently upholds it will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; but if one distorts it and acts against it, one will revolve through the six realms for countless kalpas.
With single-minded

devotion to recollecting the name of Amitābha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to the length of time, never abandoning it in thought after thought, this is called the karma of right concentration,
because it accords with that Buddha's
(Amitābha Buddha)
vow.
This is an instruction of Master Shandao in his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra,
devoted specifically to how to recite the Buddha's name,

Translation: With single-minded devotion to recollecting the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, no matter how long or brief the time, never abandoning it in thought after thought, this is called the karma of right concentration, because it is in accord with the vow of Amitābha Buddha.

[Single-minded] Master Tanluan, in his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, taught: Single-mindedness means thought following thought in an unbroken stream, without a single other thought intermingled in between. (See
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings

) [Never abandoning it] Every thought is the name of Amitābha. [Right concentration] Correct meditation; the body and mind purified and free from distraction is called "right concentration". [Karma] The activity of body, speech, and mind. [Because it accords with that Buddha's vow] "With single-minded devotion recollecting the name of Amitābha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to the length of time, never abandoning it in thought after thought" - this is because it accords with the vow of Amitābha Buddha.
Master Shandao is the incarnation of Amitābha, and his words are the words of Amitābha Buddha. From this we know that sentient beings who
recite the Buddha single-mindedly, never abandoning it in thought after thought,
this is to accord with the vow of the Buddha (Amitābha Buddha). Then,
recitation with a distracted mind runs counter to the Buddha's vow!
[Distracted recitation] Reciting the Buddha's name with the mouth while the mind thinks of other things.
With regard to distracted recitation,
Master Hanshan taught in his Song of Wasted Effort:
Reciting Amitābha with the mouth while the mind is scattered, though one shouts the throat hoarse, it is all in vain.”
[Song of Wasted Effort] “

Fèi means to spend time and effort; xián means useless and a waste of effort. Fèi xián means spending time and effort with no actual result - what is commonly called doing work in vain. In the Song of Wasted Effort, Master Hanshan points out the common pitfalls of wasted effort in practice and how to get out of them.
(See
Annotation on the Song of Wasted Effort
Here I transcribe this passage of Master Hanshan's teaching and annotate it as follows:

[To recite the Buddha's name is easy, to have faith is hard; when heart and mouth do not agree, all is wasted toil; to recite Amitābha while the mind is scattered, though the throat be shouted hoarse, is all in vain.]

Reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a sincere, genuine heart is hard; when heart and mouth are not one (the heart not genuine: the mouth recites the Buddha while the mind thinks of other things), it is always wasted (all in vain); reciting Amitābha Buddha while the mind thinks of other things, shouting the throat hoarse is also to no avail.

[Genuine faith] A heart of truth and sincerity; when heart and mouth are not one, it is false. Therefore the next line says "when heart and mouth are not one, all is wasted (all in vain)". The "faith" here is not the faith of faith-vow-practice, but the sense of being truthful and sincere.
For example, a "trade wind" (xìn fēng) is a wind that comes on schedule each year once a certain season arrives - a wind of sincerity and faithfulness.

[Truthful and sincere] Honest, not deceiving. [Though one shout the throat hoarse, all is in vain] Because "reciting Amitābha with the mouth while the mind is scattered (distracted recitation)" cannot accomplish the ten continuous recitations at the moment of death (this is the minimum requirement for rebirth, see
The Conditions for Rebirth
), so one cannot attain rebirth; all is wasted effort.
Master Hanshan points this out with piercing clarity:
“Reciting Amitābha while the mind is scattered
(distracted recitation)
, though one shouts the throat hoarse, it is all in vain.”
Question: What is reciting the Buddha with a gathered mind?
Answer: Gathering the mind means bringing the mind to focus on a single object, without distraction or torpor. So gathered-mind recitation is single-minded recitation. Master Yinguang taught:
“Gathering the mind to recite the Buddha is a way that is fixed and cannot be altered.”
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
Letter to Layman Liu Guanshan, No. 1)
Question: What is the difference between single-minded recitation of the Buddha and single-minded recitation of the name?

Answer: There are four kinds of reciting the Buddha: 1. Reciting the name, focusing solely on calling the Buddha's name; 2. Reciting while contemplating an image, gazing upon the Buddha's image while calling the name; 3. Reciting through visualization, contemplating the Buddha's thirty-two marks and his merits; 4. Reciting through the contemplation of true reality, deeply contemplating the true nature of all phenomena, which is the Buddha's Dharmakāya. Since people of this age who recite the Buddha do so basically by reciting the name, "reciting the Buddha" in common speech refers to reciting the name. In this way, single-minded recitation of the Buddha and single-minded recitation of the name are synonymous. In Master Shandao's age, however, there were still many who practiced visualization-recitation, but because the object was subtle and the mind coarse, the consciousness scattered and the spirit wandered, so accomplishment was rare. Therefore Master Shandao particularly promoted recitation of the name, and gave a specific instruction:

“Question: Why not have them practice contemplation, but instead directly urge them to call the name single-mindedly? Answer: Because sentient beings are heavy with hindrances, the object is subtle and the mind coarse, the consciousness scatters and the spirit wanders, so contemplation is difficult to accomplish. Thus the Great Sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)

in his compassion directly urged them to call the name single-mindedly. Precisely because calling the name is easy, continuity brings rebirth. If one can sustain thought after thought continuously, making the end of life the limit,
(one who thus practices for a lifetime)

, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why? Because there are no external distracting conditions, one gains right mindfulness, being in accord with the Buddha's primal vow, not going against the teaching, and following the Buddha's words.”
(See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
Continuity brings rebirth.
If one can
sustain thought after thought without interruption,
making the end of life the very limit,
then
of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.
May all beings, upon right reflection, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, must
rouse themselves and restrain themselves,
never abandoning day or night,
so that as the last thought ends life, the next thought is immediately reborn.
Ever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma joy,
and even attaining Buddhahood,
how could this not be joy indeed!
[Continuity] The thoughts of reciting the Buddha are linked together, not interrupted by deluded thoughts.
This is an instruction of Master Shandao in his Doctrine of the Two Kinds of Practice - the Specific and the Miscellaneous,
devoted specifically to how to cultivate
so as to surely
attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Master Yinguang, the manifestation of Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
greatly praised this passage, saying:
Venerable Shandao is the incarnation of Amitābha,
possessing great supernatural powers and great wisdom. In spreading the Pure Land teaching, he did not esteem the profound and mysterious, but only rested on the sincere, real, and plain,
instructing people how to cultivate.
As for
the Doctrine of Specific and Miscellaneous Practice that he set forth, its benefit is inexhaustible.
(The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Letter to the brothers of a certain Layman Yongjia). Here I annotate it as follows:
Precisely because calling the name is easy,
continuity brings rebirth.
If one can
sustain thought after thought without interruption,
making the end of life the limit,
that person
who thus practices for a lifetime
, of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.]
Precisely because recitation of the name is easier to accomplish than recitation through visualization,
when the moment of death comes, as long as one's thoughts of reciting the Buddha are continuous,
(not interrupted by deluded thoughts)
, one at once attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
If one can keep the thoughts of reciting the Buddha continuous and thus practice for a lifetime, then of ten people, ten are reborn; of a hundred people, a hundred are reborn.
[Continuity brings rebirth.]
“Continuity brings rebirth” means:
when the moment of death comes, if the thoughts of reciting the Buddha are continuous,
(not interrupted by deluded thoughts)
, one at once attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The "continuity" here is what the Surangama Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva calls
“pure thoughts succeeding one another,”

that is, the thoughts of reciting the Buddha following one another in succession, without a single deluded thought mixed in the midst (if a deluded thought is mixed in, it is no longer continuity). One must not mistake the two characters "continuity" here as referring to the sound of the Buddha-name being continuous in the mouth (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind). This is what is meant by "a hair's breadth of error leading to a thousand miles of divergence." [Sustaining thought after thought, making the end of life the limit] Because when the moment of death comes, continuous thoughts of reciting the Buddha bring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, therefore one should practice thus throughout one's whole life,
making the thoughts of reciting the Buddha continuous, and the repeated practice becoming one's very nature,

. In this way one will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss - of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. [Repeated practice becoming nature] It means that through constant and repeated practice, one makes the continuity of reciting the Buddha become a natural habit.
[May all beings, upon right reflection, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, must rouse themselves and restrain themselves, never abandoning day or night.]
May
all beings,
upon right reflection, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
truly
must
rouse and restrain themselves,
not ceasing the continuity of thought after thought by day or night,

[Rousing oneself and restraining oneself] Rousing the mind means spurring one's heart to do what ought to be done; restraining oneself means curbing oneself from doing what ought not to be done. The four characters "rouse the mind and restrain oneself" are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and sweeping away obstacles.
[As the last thought ends life, the next thought is immediately reborn. Ever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma joy, and even attaining Buddhahood - how could this not be joy indeed!]
Practicing thus,
as the last thought ends life, the next thought is immediately reborn
in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss,
. Ever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma joy, and even attaining Buddhahood - how could this not be joy indeed!

[As the last thought ends life, the next thought is immediately reborn] This means: because the thoughts of reciting the Buddha are continuous, the very last thought at death is necessarily a thought of reciting the Buddha,
and after that last thought,
one is immediately reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings in the ten directions call upon my name and wish to be reborn in my land,
even down to ten recitations
(even down to ten continuous recitations at the moment of death),
if they should not be reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
This is an instruction of Master Shandao in his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra,
devoted specifically to the conditions for rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Even down to ten recitations]
The "even down to ten recitations" spoken of here, taken together with Master Shandao's instruction above on
“never abandoning it in thought after thought”
and
“sustaining thought after thought, making the end of life the limit,”
makes it clearly known that this is
“extending up to a whole life
(one whole lifetime)
of continuous thought after thought, and down to
ten continuous recitations at the moment of death”
as a condensed expression. For Master Shandao has already clearly said:
“never abandoning it in thought after thought”
and
“sustaining thought after thought, making the end of life the limit,”
and
“never abandoning it in thought after thought”
and
“sustaining thought after thought, making the end of life the limit,”
are precisely for the sake of making the thoughts continuous and the repeated practice become one's nature,
so as to ensure the ten continuous recitations at the moment of death.
If one recited the Buddha in daily life but does not recite at death, or recites at death but with a distracted mind, these are all not
“never abandoning it in thought after thought”
and
“sustaining thought after thought, making the end of life the limit.”
Therefore, the meaning of "even down to ten recitations" is
“even down to ten continuous recitations at the moment of death.”
This kind of condensed rhetoric is found everywhere in classical Chinese; therefore
“even down to ten recitations, if one is not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
means precisely:
ten recitations at the moment of death, and continuity brings rebirth.
[Ten recitations] Reciting ten phrases of the Buddha's name.
[Sustaining thought after thought, repeated practice becoming nature] Through constant and repeated practice, making the continuity of thought after thought become a natural habit.

Master Shandao is the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, and his words are the words of Amitābha Buddha. How one may attain rebirth is of course based on his words as the standard - this is the authority of the sacred word. Reciters of the Buddha must engrave this upon their hearts, believing it all the more, and relying on it all the more.

Note: In Master Shandao's age, through the teaching of the three generations of patriarchs - Master Tanluan, Master Daochuo, and Master Shandao - the ten continuous recitations at death being the condition for rebirth had already become the consensus of the reciters of the Buddha of that time, and indeed their most basic common knowledge.
Therefore
“even down to ten recitations, if one is not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
clearly means:
ten recitations at the moment of death, and continuity brings rebirth.
Unless one is a hopelessly ignorant outsider or a malicious slanderer of the Dharma, one would never
twist “even down to ten recitations, if one is not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”

into "if one recites the Buddha ten times with a distracted mind in daily life, one attains rebirth." That is why Master Shandao adopted the condensed expression "even down to ten recitations," making the whole sentence concise and well-formed, pleasant to read aloud and easy to memorize.
Furthermore, Master Shandao made it very clear:
continuity brings rebirth.
If one can
sustain thought after thought, making the end of life the limit,
then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.
May all beings, upon right reflection, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, must
rouse themselves and restrain themselves
(spur themselves on and hold themselves back)
never abandoning day or night
(not ceasing the continuity of thought after thought by day or night)
, so that as the last thought ends life, the next thought is immediately reborn. Ever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma joy, and even attaining Buddhahood - how could this not be joy indeed!
(See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
If "reciting the Buddha ten times with a distracted mind in daily life brings rebirth," why would Master Shandao need to say
“continuity brings rebirth”
And why
would he need to say
“sustaining thought after thought, making the end of life the limit”
? And why
would he need to say
“whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse and restrain oneself, never abandoning by day or night”
? Therefore Huijing, Jingzong, and others who
twist “even down to ten recitations, if one is not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
into "if one recites the Buddha ten times with a distracted mind in daily life, one attains rebirth" (and so loudly proclaim that "calling the name surely brings rebirth") are completely wrong.
As for
the conditions for rebirth, the sage Master Tanluan, who had realized the fruit of practice, taught:
(See
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
With no other thought intermingling, thought following thought
(in succession)
, extending to ten recitations, this is called the ten recitations in continuity.
If the ten recitations at the moment of death are continuous, one attains rebirth.
As for
the conditions for rebirth, the sage Master Daochuo, who had realized the fruit of practice, taught:
(See
Master Daochuo's Pure Land Teachings
If there are sentient beings who, even if they have committed evil throughout their lives,
at the moment of death, with ten recitations in continuity,
call upon my name,
if they are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Question: Master Daochuo's instruction above says:

“If there are sentient beings who, even if they have committed evil throughout their lives, at the moment of death, with ten recitations in continuity, call upon my name, if they are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

Since "even if one has committed evil throughout one's life," as long as "at the moment of death the ten recitations are in continuity," one will surely be reborn - then reciters of the Buddha need not abandon evil and do good. Is this so?
Answer:
“Even if one has committed evil throughout one's life, as long as at the moment of death the ten recitations are in continuity, one will surely be reborn”

, this shows that right mindfulness at death (the ten recitations in continuity) is of vital importance; that is to say: the ten continuous recitations at death are the sole requirement for rebirth. As long as the ten recitations at the moment of death are continuous, one can move Amitābha Buddha to come and welcome one.

But to achieve this requirement, one must in daily life make the ten recitations in continuity become one's nature through repeated practice, and abandoning evil and doing good are very important auxiliary conditions. Therefore Master Shandao taught:
“May all beings, upon right reflection, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
must rouse and restrain themselves,

never abandoning day or night. So that as the last thought ends life, the next thought is immediately reborn. Ever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma joy, and even attaining Buddhahood - how could this not be joy indeed!”
In this teaching, the
“rouse and restrain oneself”

means spurring oneself on and holding oneself back. A person who indulges himself in doing evil is unable to "rouse and restrain himself," and moreover is not in accord with the single-minded recitation of the Buddha unmixed with deluded thoughts.
On this, the Repentance Master Ciyun taught:
“When the mind is thus bound to the Buddha, it naturally and constantly screens off all evil thoughts. If one is about to do evil, because one recollects the Buddha, the evil cannot come to be.”
The Two Gateways for Resolving Doubts and Practicing the Vows of Rebirth in the Pure Land

Therefore, a person who does not rouse and restrain himself can hardly make the ten continuous recitations become one's nature through repeated practice, and so the ten continuous recitations at the moment of death are not guaranteed. On the contrary, if one truly makes the ten continuous recitations become one's nature through repeated practice, one will not go on committing evil, because
“if one is about to do evil, because one recollects the Buddha, the evil cannot come to be.”

Though there are also extremely rare exceptions - those who committed evil throughout life yet accomplished "ten recitations in continuity at the moment of death." This occurs with practitioners who in a former life already possessed considerable skill, but because they had not yet eradicated the delusions of views and thought, they transmigrated into this life. In this life they again wandered onto a wrong path and did evil all their lives. At the moment of death, through the guidance of a good friend, they awoke at once, repented with utmost sincerity, and accomplished the ten recitations in continuity and were reborn. Consider: if not based upon the bodhi-mind and profound skill from a former life, how, at the moment of death amid the pressing torment of all suffering, could one suddenly give rise to faith and vow and abruptly accomplish the ten recitations in continuity?

Therefore one must never imitate this, because such a case is hardly one in ten thousand of those who are reborn. Consider: if in daily life one indulges one's behavior, letting the mind do evil, and the moment adverse or favorable circumstances arise, the mind follows them and does as it pleases, then at the moment of death amid the pressing torment of all suffering, how could one accomplish the ten recitations in continuity? On this principle, since ancient times the patriarchs and great masters have given very many teachings and discussions.
Question: There is a saying: "Even though one recites the Buddha with a distracted mind, as long as faith and vow are complete, one will surely be reborn." Is this saying correct?
Answer: The Buddha and the patriarchs have taught again and again to recite the Buddha single-mindedly, and have reiterated again and again to practice as instructed (see
Annotation on the Sutra of the Buddha's Praise of the Pure Land
). Therefore, one whose faith and vow are complete is necessarily one who practices as instructed and recites the Buddha single-mindedly (see
Reciting Single-Mindedly, Not with a Distracted Mind
). One who recites with a distracted mind is, because of fearing difficulty and hardship, acting contrary to the teaching of the Buddha and the patriarchs,
which is precisely a concrete expression of faith not being true and vow not being earnest.
Therefore, one who recites with a distracted mind certainly does not have complete faith and vow.

[One who recites with a distracted mind certainly does not have complete faith and vow] Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, taught in his Collection of the Myriad Good Deeds All Returning to One:
“If one's words and actions do not correspond,
and the power of faith is slight,
without a thought of continuous thought after thought, but with a mind of frequent interruptions
(that is, reciting with a distracted mind),
Relying on his indolence,
hoping at death to be reborn, but blocked by the hindrance of karma, he will probably not meet a good friend; assailed by wind and fire (the dissolution of the elements),
right mindfulness is not accomplished.”

In this teaching, Master Yongming points out clearly: why does one recite with a distracted mind ("without a thought of continuous thought after thought, but with a mind of frequent interruptions")? It is because of
“words and actions not corresponding, and the power of faith being slight.”

Therefore, one whose words and actions correspond and whose faith and vow are sincere and earnest will surely recite single-mindedly. But reciting with a distracted mind precisely shows that such a person is "of words and actions not corresponding, and power of faith slight." Moreover, Master Yongming specifically points out: distracted recitation is an act of indolence, and continuing in this indolence (
“relying on his indolence”
), at the moment of death
“assailed by wind and fire, right mindfulness is not accomplished,”

and therefore one cannot attain rebirth. [Words and actions not corresponding] Words and actions do not match: in speech one says one has true faith and earnest vows, but in actual action one is indolent (neither true nor earnest):
“without a thought of continuous thought after thought, but with a mind of frequent interruptions.”
[Probably not meeting a good friend] It is feared that one will hardly meet a great good friend who can support him in accomplishing right mindfulness at death.

“Even though one recites with a distracted mind, as long as faith and vow are complete” means: reciting with a distracted mind while faith and vow are complete. But such a state as "reciting with a distracted mind while faith and vow are complete" does not exist at all; it is a false proposition, just as there is no such thing as a brave warrior who flinches on the battlefield. Since such a state does not exist, how can one speak of the matter of rebirth or no rebirth? Therefore, "even though one recites with a distracted mind, as long as faith and vow are complete, one will surely be reborn" is fundamentally an absurdity.
[False proposition] A proposition that is not true. [Proposition] A declarative sentence expressing a judgment.
Question: Circulating on the internet is the “Master Hōnen's
Phrases” (also titled “Dharma Words on Reassuring Recitation of the Buddha”), selected by Master Huijing from the Complete Works of Master Hōnen. The first item reads:
The karma of right concentration is precisely calling the Buddha's name; calling the name surely attains rebirth, because it relies on the Buddha's primal vow.”
May I ask: Is calling the Buddha's name precisely the karma of right concentration? Does calling the Buddha's name rely on the Buddha's (Amitābha Buddha's) primal vow?
Answer: It should be:
with single-minded
calling the Buddha's name is the karma of right concentration,
and with single-minded
calling the Buddha's name is relying on the Buddha's (Amitābha Buddha's) primal vow.
As for
“the karma of right concentration,”
the original words of Master Shandao in his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra are:
With single-minded
devotion recollecting the name of Amitābha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to the length of time,
never abandoning it in thought after thought,
this is called
right concentration
karma,
because it accords with that Buddha's vow.”
Master Hōnen, however, with ulterior motives, took this teaching,
cut off the most crucial
“single-minded”
two characters
, and
falsified it into:
The karma of right concentration is precisely calling the Buddha's name; calling the name surely attains rebirth, because it relies on the Buddha's primal vow.”
Single-mindedness

- this is the key to correct practice in the Pure Land school. Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, taught: reciting sutras, visualizing, recollecting, prostrating to the Buddha, reciting the Buddha, and praising and offering - these must be
single-minded,
and only then are they right practices.
Master Shandao said:

“Now there are two kinds of practice: first, right practices; second, miscellaneous practices. As for right practices: to single-mindedly rely on the scriptures of rebirth and practice accordingly - this is called right practice. What are they?
With single-minded
devotion to reciting this Contemplation Sutra, Amitābha Sutra, Immeasurable Life Sutra, and so on;
with single-minded
concentration on contemplating, observing, and recollecting the two kinds of adornments of that land. If prostrating, then
with single-minded
devotion prostrates to that Buddha; if calling the name, then
with single-minded
devotion calls that Buddha's name; if praising and offering, then
with single-minded
devotion praises and offers.
This is called right practice.”
(Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra)
Therefore, Master Shandao was saying
single-mindedly
calling the Buddha's name is the karma of right concentration,

but Master Hōnen falsified it into: calling the Buddha's name is the karma of right concentration. The mind dwelling on a single object is called "concentration." I ask: without single-mindedness, how could it be
right concentration?
With a distracted mind reciting the Buddha and thoughts racing without end, where does
right concentration

come from? Without right concentration, where is the karma of right concentration? It is common to see Huijing, Jingzong, and others who loudly promote distracted recitation and "calling the name surely brings rebirth" going everywhere preaching that their practice is the karma of right concentration - truly shameless boasting!
In this instruction Master Shandao states it most clearly:
single-minded
invocation of the Name — this is what conforms to the Buddha's primal vow.
Yet Master Hōnen took the most crucial
“single-minded”

and cut off both words, altering it into: “invoking the Buddha-name is itself conforming to the Buddha's primal vow,” and so reached the absurd conclusion that “invoking the name surely brings rebirth,” declaring loudly that “invocation surely assures rebirth”! Read this Words of the Dharma side by side with
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
, and
you will plainly see how Master Hōnen tampered with Master Shandao's teaching to establish the school of the primal vow
. For eight hundred years, who knows how many practitioners of Buddha-recitation it has misled, harming their lives of wisdom!

Q: Why must one have right mindfulness at the moment of death (the ten recollections continuing at death) to attain rebirth? Amitabha Buddha's five kalpas of reflection and measureless kalpas of practice — his entire great vow is to save every sentient being. With such a great compassionate heart, would he not, at the moment of our death, display his spiritual power and vow-force to receive and guide us?
A:

At the moment of death of every sentient being, Amitabha Buddha is receiving and guiding. It is only that sentient beings without right mindfulness at the moment of death cannot see it, and so follow their own deluded thoughts and, in accord with their karma, go to be reborn elsewhere.
So one must have right mindfulness at the moment of death in order to see Amitabha Buddha come to receive and guide, and to follow the Buddha to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
On this principle, Master Zhongfeng, honored as the ancient Buddha of the south of the Yangtze, instructs in his The Three Periods of Mind-Connection:
“Although it is said that Amitabha takes hold of sentient beings and brings them to rebirth, one must believe
that it is only manifesting in accord with one's own mind
the mutual response of mind and way
, and in the end
(after all)
is not obtained from outside

[It is only manifesting in accord with one's own mind] Amitabha Buddha, coming to receive (take hold of) sentient beings, manifests only in accord with one's own mind — this is due to the mutual response of mind and way, and is not obtained from outside. So only one with right mindfulness at death can see the Buddha come, while the others around do not see it.

For those dying sentient beings who lack right mindfulness at death, since there is no responsive stimulus, naturally Amitabha Buddha's receiving does not manifest in their minds, and so they too do not see the Buddha come — not that Amitabha Buddha did not come to receive them.
So whether or not one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at death
(the ten recollections continuing at death)
This is why

. This is the Buddha's own teaching!
[Mutual response of mind and way] The response of sentient beings and the response of Amitabha Buddha interpenetrate.

On the principle of mind and way mutually responding at the moment of death, Master Yinguang, the incarnation of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, instructs in the Preface to the Guide to Pure Land Practice for Beginners:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vow and with utmost sincerity move the Buddha, then the Buddha responds — as when the water is clear, the moon appears. If the mind is not pure, not sincere, is in accord with greed, anger, and delusion, and runs counter to the Buddha, it is like turbid, stirred water, and although the moon does not fail to shine upon it, it cannot be clearly reflected.”

Vernacular: The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vow and with utmost sincerity move the Buddha, then the Buddha responds — as when the water is clear and still, the moon appears (a metaphor for the pure mind of right mindfulness manifesting the receiving of Amitabha Buddha). If the mind is not pure, not sincere, is in accord with greed, anger, and delusion, and runs counter to the Buddha, it is like turbid, stirred water; although the Buddha-moon does not fail to shine upon it (a metaphor that Amitabha Buddha is always receiving every dying sentient being), yet it cannot be clearly reflected (a metaphor that a stirred, turbid, disordered mind cannot manifest the receiving of Amitabha Buddha,
but instead follows its own deluded thoughts and, in accord with its karma, goes to be reborn elsewhere

“Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is turbid and stirred it hides. The moon is certainly without accepting and rejecting; that it does not appear is because the water is murky and churning, having no way to receive its reflection.”

Vernacular: Only when the water is clear and still does the moon's reflection appear; when the water is turbid and stirred, the reflection does not appear. The moon certainly shines without accepting and rejecting; that it does not appear is because the water is murky and churning, with no way to receive its reflection. (Metaphor: only those sentient beings with right mindfulness at death can see the receiving of Amitabha Buddha, while those without right mindfulness at death cannot see the receiving of Amitabha Buddha. Amitabha Buddha certainly receives every dying sentient being without accepting or rejecting; that those without right mindfulness at death cannot see his receiving is because
their own minds are murky
and disordered,
and so
they follow their own deluded thoughts and, in accord with their karma, go to be reborn elsewhere

So for the practitioner of Buddha-recitation, single-minded right mindfulness at the moment of death is extremely important. One who recites a thousand times, ten thousand times, even all day and all year — does so for nothing other than to make this single thought of recitation familiar,
to ensure that at the moment of death this thought continues without break, and that it manifests the receiving of Amitabha Buddha
. Therefore Master Shandao, the incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, and Master Yongming, also an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, both earnestly instruct:
to accomplish the ten recollections continuing at death
(see
The Conditions for Rebirth
This is the measure of holy speech! If one does not listen to the words of Amitabha Buddha, whose words will one listen to?

[Continuing (xiāng xù)] The thought of recitation follows on without break, unmingled with deluded thoughts. [Measure of holy speech] This is what the sages have spoken — correct and without error, certainly to be received in faith.
